query: which states decoupled from the federal 100% bonus depreciation for 2026
intent_note: List of states that don't conform to restored 100% bonus depreciation for tax year 2026, for the fund's state filings.

States Decoupled from 100% Bonus Depreciation (2026)
California: Decouples via static IRC conformity and requires a full add-back of federal bonus depreciation.
Connecticut: Decouples from bonus depreciation add-backs (with some rules differing by tax type/year).
Delaware: Enacted legislation (HB 255) decoupling from post-OBBBA bonus depreciation changes, retaining pre-OBBBA rules for affected property through 2030.
District of Columbia: Decouples from federal bonus depreciation.
Georgia: Decouples from IRC § 168(k) bonus depreciation.
Hawaii: Decouples from IRC § 168(k).
Idaho: Decouples from IRC § 168(k) bonus depreciation.
Illinois: Decouples from federal bonus depreciation and requires an add-back of the § 168(k) deduction (with specific statutory subtractions/modifications).
Indiana: Decouples from bonus depreciation add-backs.
Maryland: Decouples from federal bonus depreciation.
New Hampshire: Decouples on its business profits tax (with no personal income tax).
New Jersey: Decouples and requires an add-back.
New Mexico: Decoupled under SB 151 (effective May 20, 2026), requiring an add-back and regular depreciation schedules.
New York (and New York City): Decouples from federal bonus depreciation and requires add-backs/modifications (with narrow exceptions such as certain Liberty/Resurgence Zone property).
Oregon: Decoupled for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026 under SB 1507, requiring an add-back and recovery over time.
Pennsylvania: Decouples from federal bonus depreciation.
Rhode Island: Decouples from bonus depreciation.
South Carolina: Does not adopt IRC § 168(k) bonus depreciation.
Virginia: Remains decoupled from § 168(k) bonus depreciation.
States with Partial Conformity or Mixed Treatment
Some jurisdictions allow partial expensing, spread add-backs over multiple years, or decouple for only one taxpayer type—for example, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina (which allows a portion upfront and deducts the add-back over five years), and Ohio, as well as Arizona (where treatment differs between individuals and corporations).
